review:
So, after about 8.5 hours of gameplay, I finally got to the "soft endgame" of the Early Alpha build - the Insect stage.
My impressions are sort of... mixed, and here's why.

The game on normal difficulty plays a lot like Subnautica on peaceful mode - no enemies, no real hazards aside from fall damage and occasional meteor showers, and I haven't died once to asphyxiation or thirst yet. It [b]also[/b] plays like Factorio or maybe Satisfactory, with how much you have to build and craft, but don't expect sprawling factories or massive mining plants - all the resources are literally lying around and you have to run and mine them No Man's Sky style.

Graphics are phenomenal, as is performance - I did not expect it to run on max settings with over 60 FPS on an RTX 2060 with so much foliage and water and whatnot. A lot of my idle time was spent just admiring the scenery and whizzing around the world on a jetpack.

Speaking of jetpack. This currently is [b]the only[/b] mode of transportation in the game with infinite fuel, and as soon as I got it, the game got massively easier. It also got me clipping into a lot of cliffs and weird places, which was also really fun :D I would prefer something like an electric buggy, with the jetpack running on biofuel or something for the sake of balance, but as it's Alpha, it's really not an issue.

What I really didn't like, and I hope the devs will fix in the future, is the bad use of scientific measurements as progress bars. Here's a TL;DR.

When you reach the (currently endgame) Insect stage (presumably when animal life starts to flourish), your planet has roughly 2 Pascals of atmospheric pressure, some 20 mK (0.02 K) of heat and 10 ppm of oxygen.
On their own, these numbers don't say anything, but here's what we have on Earth: 101325 Pascals of pressure, 293 K of temperature and 209460 ppm of oxygen.
Our planet literally has: [b]an atmosphere 50 thousand times less dense than Earth, close to absolute zero in temperature and oxygen content fit for a vacuum chamber somewhere in a lab[/b]. This is not livable, and makes absolutely zero sense when you look at it from a scientific perspective.

It also made me laugh a lot, when I saw grass and liquid water outside in what is essentially -273 C (-459.7 F) and no atmosphere to speak of.

Altogether, I recommend it. It's addictive, plays really well, and aside from that one flaw, is probably one of the better terraforming games out there. Worth a demo try or even a buy, if you're into it.

I've been playing this game since very early access. I have watched how its grown and improved over time and how they listened to what they're community was saying and requesting. [i]TL:DR - For $20, you get about 40 hours of content in the game's current state. I think the price is fair for what you get, but sales are always nice. The game is a mix between No Man's Sky and Subnautica. [b]Planet Crafter[/b] is relaxing with no enemies or threats (other than keeping water, food, and oxygen levels up). The end game needs more content, but the game stands out in the genre for its unique terraforming gameplay. I recommend it, though I have some issues with the game's pacing, which I’ll point out below. Review will be edited if a content update changes my opinion.[/i]

The game is great, and as you can see from the reviews, everyone agrees. I played [b]Planet Crafter[/b] for just under 40 hours pretty consistently over the past few days, and I really enjoyed it, but I got bored in the end-game. In this review, I won’t focus on the usual aspects like graphics, story, or performance. Instead, I want to talk about the pacing, which is the biggest area that I think could be improved.

[h3]First, a few nitpicks and notes (in case a dev reads this):[/h3]
[list]
[*]The game is open-world but not procedurally generated. This isn’t a problem, but it limits replayability.
[*]The music is atmospheric but becomes repetitive quickly. It doesn’t match the game’s tone, so I ended up muting it and playing my own. It would be nice if the music evolved with the terraforming stages.
[*]Exploration can feel like a slog until you can build a teleporter or unlock the T3 jetpack.
[*]The art/graphics are mediocre compared to other similar games, but they get the job done.
[*]If you launch two rockets in close succession, they crash hilariously.
[*]The rocks left behind by asteroids cause major frustration. They should disappear after a short time, or players should have a tool to remove them. Half the time, you can’t pick up the materials they leave behind, especially from pulsar asteroids.
[*]In the late game, you shouldn’t have to eat or drink as much as earlier stages. We need upgrades to make this process less tedious.
[/list]
[u]Now on to the "pacing." What do I mean by pacing?[/u] Pacing, to me, is how smoothly the game flows from the early game to mid-game and then into the end-game content. In [b]Planet Crafter[/b], there are distinct stages of terraforming, and I’ll focus on how well the game transitions between these stages. Note: Minor spoilers ahead.

[h3]Early Game:[/h3]
The early game is easily the best part of [b]Planet Crafter[/b]. You gather resources, build machines, and feel a real sense of progress as new tools and upgrades unlock. At this stage, you’re still tied to your base because oxygen depletes rapidly, but there’s plenty to do at home. Seeing that first hint of a blue sky is a very rewarding moment. The excitement of upgrading your gear, unlocking second-tier machines, and starting to automate parts of your terraforming process is fantastic.

Aluminum is the biggest hurdle at this stage because it’s scarce, and super alloy feels like a special treasure. You’re also balancing power generation with the tier 2 solar panels, which are pricey. The early game has excellent pacing for a survival game—you work for your progress, and it feels earned.

[h3]Mid Game:[/h3]
As the ice begins to melt, you can access more areas and materials. By now, you’re no longer starved for aluminum, sulfur, or iridium, and you’ve probably launched a few rockets to boost your terraforming progress. You’re also starting to plant grass and flowers around the landscape. Rockets drop asteroids that provide materials, and exploration becomes more viable as your equipment improves.

This is where I have my first major critique: there’s no vehicle, and the jetpack isn’t much faster than walking. Transporting materials back and forth becomes tedious, and I wish the teleporter unlocked earlier in the game. By the time you get it, it feels like you don’t need it as much anymore. The game starts to slow down toward the end of the mid-game, but the end-game is where it really stalls.

[i]If a dev reads this: Please make the rocks left behind by asteroids disappear quickly so we can harvest the materials they drop. I had a rock block my base door, and it sucked to have to reload the game just to get rid of it.[/i]

[h3]End Game:[/h3]
In the end-game, you’re waiting for your terraforming numbers to climb, but the pace slows to a crawl. By this point, you have access to every material, and your base is fully self-sufficient. You can mine everything, gather food from your farms, and produce water with ease. If your base is well-built, it runs smoothly, and you’re no longer in any real danger.

But here’s the issue: by now, you’re just waiting. Unlocks come very slowly, and there’s not much left to do besides building more machines and watching the terraforming numbers go up. I found myself going AFK or watching YouTube while waiting for things to happen. The gameplay loop becomes stale. You can only build so many machines or base structures before it feels monotonous. This is where [b]Planet Crafter[/b] falters in terms of pacing. It’s not just about content—it's about how the game progresses from one phase to another.

[u]So how do the devs improve this?[/u] I think the transition between terraforming stages should be compressed. More machines and content in the late game would help keep players engaged. Some crafting recipes could also be more complex, requiring players to work a bit harder for materials, but with faster payoffs. This would give the game a better sense of progression. Satisfactory is a great example of a game with well-paced content from start to finish.

Overall, [b]Planet Crafter[/b] is a great game that you should definitely try if you enjoy this genre. For a small indie studio, this game is a massive achievement. It plays well, there are few bugs, and it’s a relaxing experience. For me, the biggest issue is the pacing—getting from point A to B feels fine, but moving from B to C takes far too long, and there’s not enough to do in between. You can explore, build more machines, and expand your base, but it all starts to feel repetitive.

That said, I still recommend this title, and I’ll be returning to it when more content drops.

Gave me the 'Minecraft for the first time' feeling, something I never thought I'd feel again. It's a world to get lost in. Stuff to explore, cool bases to build, danger to avoid (asphyxiation, dehydration, starvation), and a lot of gear and blueprints to unlock that helps with all three.

800  hour Update: 5 planets now. Lots of replay value.

I’m not someone who usually leaves reviews, but I’ve put a lot of time into Planet Crafter (164 hours since February 24th) and it feels worth saying something. The game is all about landing on an empty planet and slowly turning it into somewhere you actually want to live, and that process is strangely relaxing and very addictive.

My favorite thing early on was just watching the world change. Depending on which map you’re playing, you notice small details shifting as you progress through the different stages of life on the planets, and that slow transformation is really satisfying to see.

One of my favorite things is the different game modes. I really like that you can choose Relaxed mode and the game is still engaging and gives you goals and little challenges to work toward, instead of feeling boring or “easy mode.” It lets you decide how stressful or chill you want the experience to be without losing the sense of progression.

I also appreciate that there is still a lot to do even after you “complete” terraforming—there are more systems to unlock, places to explore, and things to build, so it never feels like the game just ends the moment the planet turns green.

If you enjoy building, exploring, and watching a world change over time at your own pace, this is a great game to sink into.

Planet Crafter is the rare survival game that looks at grinding and says: “what if this didn’t feel like unpaid labor?” and then actually follows through.

From the first oxygen gasp to watching an entire planet slowly change in ways I wish my garden would, the game turns progression into something dangerously close to JOY. Every resource run feels purposeful, every upgrade visibly reshapes the world, and suddenly you realize you’ve been grinding for hours without once muttering, “why am I doing this?” That ALONE deserves a standing ovation.

The developers clearly understood the assignment: make the numbers matter, make the wait feel earned, and make the environment I T S E L F become your reward. Seeing lakes form, skies change color (light green is my personal fave), and life creep back into a once hostile rock is wildly satisfying. It’s not just 'progress bars' filling up, it’s like Planet ASMR... But for the soul?

What really sells it is how clean and respectful the design feels. No bloated systems, no artificial frustration, no grind-for-the-sake-of-grind nonsense. Just a steady addictive loop that warrants the “just one more task” whisper you tell yourself until the sun rises in real life. The pacing feels intentional, the UI stays out of your way, and the sense of scale grows, usually alongside your ambition (or a friend you play with). You’re not farming materials, you’re terraforming a future. You’re not crafting gear, you’re rewriting the destiny of a planet. And somehow, that turns mining rocks into a deeply relaxing, oddly hopeful experience.

H U G E appreciation to the devs for creating a game where progress feels personal, effort feels rewarded, and the grind finally feels like play. They also keep releasing new DLC of different planets to terraform! At time of writing they have released Toxicity DLC, and when I finish terraforming Aqualis, you can bet I'm gonna buy that ASAP.

Highly recommended... Just don’t start it when you need to be productive tomorrow. I'm guilty of calling out of work next day just to keep playing hahaha

EDIT: As of now, I am approximately 1/3rd of the way through Toxicity, and I am really vibing the cleanup-crew style of planet crafting. It's a refreshing new take on the prior planets where your task quota is measured in both idle number climbs, as well as manual environment management. I will write more when I finish the terraformation process!

It's a 6.5/10, full of exciting surprises but also many letdowns.

PROS:
+World is *very* fun to explore
+World changes in delightful ways as game progresses
+Time spent base-building feels rewarding
+Excellent soundtrack
+High volume of unlocks, lots of content
+Relaxing crafting game with decent resource management loop 

CONS:
-Placing structures is buggy and adherence to grid is inconsistent
-Environment collision is a horrific mess, clipping inside geometry is commonplace
-Certain unlocks are virtually useless and feel like padding
-Draw distance on medium graphics settings causes extreme pop-in and important structures do not have any LoDs, rendering them invisible at a fairly close range
-Late-game crafting loop lacks useful automation and recipes for insects/frogs are extremely tedious
-Aesthetics, gameplay, and many icons are *highly* derivative of Subnautica
-Disappointing ending(s)
-Many structures/recipes/terraforming phases unlock in bizarre order depending on how you choose to increase Terraformation index
-Living creatures lack variety, animal system should be huge reward but feels underdeveloped.
-Certain mechanics do not function as expected (specifically resource miners needing very specific placement and production fuses not working on many machines that produce items i.e. food growers)
-High volume storage unlocks too late in the game
-Pinning a recipe should be a default mechanic, not an unlock.

All in all, a fun game with a very exciting first 15 hours that eventually becomes highly tedious. A vast amount of content and systems, but many elements lack a robust implementation. Well worth the money, but decidedly uneven.

A game that scratches the Subnautica itch. Terraform a planet from barren to bountiful, from uninhabitable to habitable. This game has strong depth in crafting and was addictive at times. I did feel the middle portion of the terraformation levels was somewhat boring, and I found myself without a lot of tasks to do and just waiting as my terraforming metrics went up steadily. Maybe that balancing will be fixed in the 1.0 release. 

Overall would recommend this game. I had a lot of fun.

This is a survival game, technically. In practice, it feels like survival wrapped in a warm blanket that occasionally reminds you to breathe.

There are multiple difficulty levels, but even the hardest one is very forgiving compared to most survival games. It leans hard into a sandbox,  that makes it feel surprisingly cozy. You’re not constantly being hunted or punished. You’re exploring, building, terraforming, and vibing… as long as you remember your oxygen.

And yes, you can die. Mostly from falling off very tall things/cliffs or from not paying attention to oxygen, hunger, or thirst. Which is fair. The planet isn’t cruel, it just expects you to read your gauges.

Visually, this game is gorgeous. The landscapes are peaceful and fun to explore, and watching the terraforming process slowly change the world is incredibly satisfying. Water appears, skies shift, terrain transforms. It’s like watching a dead planet wake up in real time, and I loved every minute of it.

The absolute highlight was co-op. I played with my 13-year-old son, and we had an amazing time. At one point, the outside world had no oxygen yet and I was sprinting toward our base for dear life… when he deconstructed the door. While I was running toward it. Oxygen ticking down. Absolute betrayal.

He also repeatedly emptied my neatly categorized, lovingly organized lockers because he “needed the resources.” Needed them for what? No explanation was given. I assume science. Or crime.

Despite the attempted suffocation and ongoing inventory theft, co-op worked great and added a ton of fun to the experience. Building together, exploring together, and watching the planet transform together made for some genuinely great moments.

If you’re looking for brutal survival, this may be too gentle. But if you want a beautiful, relaxing sandbox survival game where the biggest threat is forgetting to breathe or trusting your co-op partner, Planet Crafter is an easy recommendation.

10/10 would terraform again.
0/10 would trust my teammate with doors.

This game is one of the most fun games I've ever played. I have a rare neurodegenerative disease and so I don't get to do much besides play video games because I'm wheelchair bound. I have found the repetitiveness of collecting resources and building and expanding my base so relaxing and exciting. There's always something to do, and places to explore. The graphics are really good too! I just wanted to tell the devs thank you for making my time here on earth a bit easier with your awesome space game!

It is most definitely an early access game. My first 8 hours ore so were spent getting to the lakes terraformation stage, at which point I realized my base in the starter valley would soon be under water. It's at this point I would typically quit a game from discouragement, realizing all my progress was wasted and being too lazy to move my base. But it only took me a few seconds of deliberation to realize I really wanted to start a new save and do it correctly from initially loading into the new, barren, desolate world.
I started the new save, made my base on the top of a hill, and the next 32 hours have been on one save. 
What does it get right? It provides (what I find to be) a relaxing singleplayer survival game that's about steady progress and steady expansion. For my gaming habits, it strikes the proper balance of chill and engaging that I personally get lost in. (Not physically lost in my surroundings, that stopped at around 20 hrs in) Time passes and the only way I can tell is because the screens indicate my machines are contributing to the total terraformation process number that moves ceaselessly upwards.
What does it get wrong? In my exploration of nearly every corner, I find many objects that are easily clipped through, which has put me in an inescapable void one too many times. Errant geological structures aside, there's a number of issues that are present and irritating, but as the game gets closer and closer to 1.0, I'm sure the building will become more intuitive and flow better. As it stands, there is nearly too much freedom to build, and base pieces are difficult to link together at any angle other than head-on. I haven't yet found a way to repeatedly build one type of base piece, every time I place one I have to re-open the build menu and select the piece again. (This may be user error, but I don't think so. Feel free to let me know if I'm just doing something dumb.)
What about the devs? I don't know anything of the studio or developers, but I appreciate the notes they put in the update logs and they seem to care about their player base, taking small tidbits of feedback and also preserving the vision they have in their heads for the game. In the short time I've been playing, they've added QoL things that do what they intend, improve quality of life and ease little moments of previous frustration.

TLDR; If you like singleplayer survival/crafting with intense focus on exploration and progression, it's worth every penny you spend on it.

This is obviously early access. The world feels more barren than intended, the resources you gather are scattered in a way that feels odd. Their models feel out of place with just a random piece of iron laying on the ground (you do not mine nodes, you pick up singular items). World collision is poorly mapped, you can clip through most cliffs/rocks. 

However. They have "the thing" that makes the game good.  A feeling that is just right. When you've increased the atmospheric pressure enough so the sky turns blue is really satisfying. When you have increased biomass by spamming your location with grass spreaders and you see moss start to grow all over your barren world you can relax and know that this world will in time be less hostile, more habitable and a lot more welcoming to future settlers. 

TL;DR: If you can't handle some rough edges of early access please wait. If you think that game mechanics are more important than a game feeling polished this is for you.

One of my absolute favorite games ever!

The sandboxy gameplay of Planet Crafter resembles "Subnautica on land" since you need to explore a strange planet after having crashed there, you need to gather and grow ressources including many that look like scattered rocks, you'll craft and also build sci-fi-like looking bases. Plus your main goal is to leave the game world.

Like in Subnautica, you won't be given any "quests" (except for a few unrewarded tutorial "missions"), and the "story" consists mainly of messages left by those who came before you (storywise). Some of these messages will lead you to a few special locations.

It really made a difference to the gaming experience when messages were implemented that led us to hidden passages and then to the ruins of "paradise", plus the means to reveal invisible altars later on... Oh yes, and there are some more hidden underground-bases plus a few other "secrets" as well. 

However, unlike Subnautica, the planet/s of Planet Crafter can be transformed thoroughly, which was really unique at the time this game was released in Early Access. Yes, Subnautica 2 now has some regions that will also change according to your actions - however not this drastically.

It's such a pleasure to see how the barren desert game world of Planet Crafter changes step by step into lush colorfully overgrown landscapes with a gorgeous looking sky and then with a lot of different lifeforms, all of which is caused by the work of your own "hands".

It's really cool to watch how puddles start to form and then grow into lakes, how ice melts away, the water level rises (and rises, rises, and then rises even more!), how reddish sand slowly turns into green "moss" where then grass tufts start to sprout, more and more foliage pops up, then trees, even some extremely tall ones (that grow slowly, which is absolutely the best), waterfalls come gushing down, tangled roots show up that let you climb canyon walls, then multicoloured butterflies appear, fish, frogs and at the end of it all even weird sci-fi mammals...

And when the terraforming is all done, the planet is an extremely beautiful place to marvel at.

A unique task in this game is building several "base camps" along your way to provide yourself with oxygen, shelter and a place to produce water while exploring, but also storage space, food growers, etc. This is something that I have always loved to do in sandbox games, but very few games other than Planet Crafter actually require.

Like in so many other games, oxygen, water and food is required, while sleeping is not, and luckily your character can't get sick, and all damages can be cured simply by eating your veggies :D I very much appreciate that Planet Crafter is one of the rare games that won't force you to eat meat btw., not even fish. Cooking is possible too, but very optional. If cookies or cakes were more valuable for trading (by using trade rockets), I'd engage in baking a lot though :D Actually, there's just too few stuff we can trade away for good profit.

Plundering the wrecked space-ships and underground hideaways is a real fun activity though, and I simply can't stop exploring those random wreckages on portal-worlds (unlocked later in the game). I really love the designs of these wrecks too, and also the look of most things that you can craft and build in this game.

Technically the game is very well made in my opinion, I didn't find any game-breaking bugs. Merely some surface textures are still in need of improvments, since resources from meteors might get stuck or even vanish inside of rocks and the like.

Using meteors that come crashing down as a means of "respawning" resources (until you can craft extractors that will provide you with endless resources from the ground) is a great idea btw.!

You can choose one of three endings for your own story, some of which are a little mean - but you'll very likely just reload afterwards anyways in order to continue playing :P I mean, how else would you be able to travel to all the additional planets? You really shouldn't miss those!

I'd recommend Aqualis at first with its giant shell island rising from the water (what a sight!), then Selenea for giant sequoia-like trees and large domes, then Skeo with those enormous dinosaur-like skulls and bones. The unique builds and crafts you can learn on each of these planets will help speeding up terraforming the following ones. As for the priced DLCs, Toxicity is the most amazing experience in my opinion, but if it's about helpful technology, terraforming Humble before that is actually more advantageous... 

In terms of game balance, I'm not 100% happy with when exactly and in which order the tech-tree is being unlocked... But of course this is only my personal opinion.

Mainly the food grower not being available from the start (not even in customized mode) still gives me the irk. Our awesome equipment and the transport to another planet must have cost Sentinel Corps a fortune storywise, so they should at least provide us with the bare minimum we'll need to survive in order not to have wasted all the money when we die, right? Which is why I'd prefer the food grower blueprint (or maybe an additional very slowly working one?) to unlock very early, plus that one primal food pack that we once had back in very early EA.

However, I think the lack of food is perhaps implemented intentionally so that we will go exploring early on, instead of just staying in one place and building our main base for hours on end?

Finding messages on mysteriously working screens in long dead wrecks is a bit weird too, especially since our own craftable signs in Planet Crafter are sooo much smaller... Reminds me of how comprehensive our PDAs are in Subnautica, while those we can find always only contain a few message lines. This is just a small irritation though.

I've become a big fan of clean-up-games; so I prefer to pick up all the resources from the ground in Planet Crafter over time, after which the left-over large metal junk keeps bothering me, since I can't remove it :D I'd also like to deconstruct and recycle a lot more things from all the wrecks on the Planet... Luckily most furniture in the random wrecks in portal-worlds can actually be dismantled.

And one last idea: how about adding something that would explain how our buildings can produce breathable oxygen? Maybe some algae-based liquid or so that we can transfer from the escape capsule and then from one building to the others?

Numbers go up.
World looks prettier.
Receive serotonin.
Repeat.

great game, very addictive... If you're looking for a tech-savvy, realistic terraforming Mars type of experience, look elsewhere.
On the other hand, if you're looking for a game that is absorbing, but that you can just pause for a while to just look around in, then this is it.
In short, it's just beautiful. In fact it's the most beautiful game I've ever played. The designs for the plants, the animals, and the forests and plains that grow from them are wonderful.
Relaxing? Yes. Busy? Yes. Do you feel like you've really achieved something as you progress? Oh, hell, yes. You've grown a world that is so lovely you'll wish that you could leave this one behind and live there.
And I've only spent 132 hours playing it ...

Edit: Got my amphibians. Happy.

Holy o2 levels, this game is fun. I've clocked just shy of 50 hours and have thoroughly enjoyed that time spent. I'm only now waiting for new content since I've played through what's currently available. 

Some thoughts:

-  The controls are simple, though sometimes targeted placing/deconstruction is a little wonky.
-  Sometimes there are graphical glitches. Only once have I died from it (I fell into a wall. RIP.). Usually it just results in an ore being inaccessible or some weird animation that goes away once repeated.
-  The music is super cool.
-  The small tidbits of lore/story are intriguing. I really want more. 
-  I desperately want amphibians already. Please. I need some frogs in my base. 
-  The asteroid showers RNG needs some tweaking. More than once I've had 2-3 showers back to back raining down on my base. On the one hand, it's more comical than anything, but on the other, it does slow me down as I wait for them to pass.
-  I would love to see a little more visual change in some stages of terraforming. I realize that may be in the works, especially for later stages, but it's such a satisfying feeling to see things change. 
-  More decor items would be awesome, both for casual players and for those of us waiting between content updates to keep us entertained in "creating" new bases/ideas.
- On that note, none of the decor items/furniture hold any real in-game value. Would be interesting if they could provide temporary buffs like sleeping in a bed makes your hunger reduce slower, etc. 
- A day counter or some kind of time-keeping system would be nice. I'd be interested to know how many "days" I've been terraforming my planet. 

Anyway, really happy to have purchased this game, and I look forward to seeing where it goes.

An excellent, slow-paced survival-crafter game.

Pros:
* Lots and lots of secrets to discover.
* Great tech tree to unlock.
* A surprising number of biomes.
* Freaking beautiful, and great (low-annoyance) soundtracks.

Cons:
* Some of the late-game mechanics aren't explained very well. (genetics, mostly, tho that may've been because I unlocked mammals way later than I should've)
* One biome ([spoiler]rainbow caves[/spoiler]) is key to mid-to-late game progress - if you haven't found it yet, you're almost crippled by a lack of quartz varieties.  A hint towards it would have been nice.

If you enjoy SOC games, I recommend Planet Crafter - but there are a few points to be aware of.
First, the game is still early access developed by two people (afaik). I can't say I encountered any game breaking bugs, but don't expect a fully finished, AAA quality. My ony personal pain point is optimization - game seems to lag at some points. Which is normal for an EA game and restarting it fixes it, so not a big deal.

Important to note that I've been following the game for a while and they've been consistently releasing patches and adhering to their roadmap (which, you know, exists) which for me is the most important things for ea games.

The second important point to know is that, quite unique in the genre, there is no violence. You aren't fighting aliens, you aren't even evading alien water monsters (talking about you Subnautica). I believe meteors can hurt you (although I never had one fall on me, it's pretty easy to avoid them) and other than that, the only way you can die is fall damage, thirst, hunger or O2. For me, this is a unique and great experience. But not everyone might appreciate it.

Now - if you are fine with the above points, I heartily recommend the game. For me it's closest to Subnautica: You are all by yourself (Even more so, as there are no cutie fishies) and you have to figure things out. You start by trying to survive, than expand your capacity and in the meanwhile, discover the fates of others before you and discover more about the planet.

The way it works is that you have to work on improving the Heat, O2 level etc to transform the planet to be habitable. They are represented by numbers and at certain points, you unlock new recipes. You harvest resources, many of which requires exploration. You may use them by themselves, craft them into alloys etc.

Initially, I thought the game was occasionally too grindy but I started a Hardcore game in the current version and so far I haven't really felt that. Might be because I know the game better now, but I feel I had to build more stuff in previous builds.

Overall, it's pretty chill and you always have a "next target" and even if you have to wait a bit, there are ways to shorten that wait. Sometimes you'll want to do those things, other times you'll want to spend some time gathering resources, modifying your base and upgrading your equipment and time will pass quicker than you expect :) 

Anyway - like I said, if the concept sounds good to you, I definitely recommend it.
A very relaxing game, no monsters, no battles, just planning and exploration.

The Planet Crafter: A Journey to Terraforming That Completely Hooked Me

I've played The Planet Crafter for about 45 hours, and I can say for sure that it's one of the most fun and surprisingly relaxing games I've ever played. I'm almost done changing my planet, and to be honest, I'm a little sad to see it end. I've really enjoyed the whole thing.

It has been very rewarding to watch this dead, red wasteland slowly become a living, breathing ecosystem from the very beginning. You feel like you've earned every milestone, like the first blue sky, the first lake forming near your base, and the first blades of grass breaking through the sand. It never gets old to see that you're making progress.

The gameplay loop really clicked with me because I like systems, automation, and building things quickly. You start small, making heaters and oxygen tanks by hand. But soon you have auto-crafters, drones, and full production lines that make the planet almost run itself. The game really shines when you go from manually surviving to managing an ecosystem automatically.

But what surprised me the most was how calm everything feels. You don't have to worry about fighting or real danger; you can just enjoy the quiet rhythm of building, optimizing, and exploring. After work, I've played this game to relax by mining resources, building up my base, and watching the world come to life around me. It's meditative in the best way possible.

The graphics are simple, but they look great when things start to grow. I still get a real sense of awe when I see rain or step into a new biome that is covered in green. The music fits that mood perfectly: calm, ambient, and hopeful.

If I had to pick on something, I'd say that the pacing of the endgame can slow down a little, especially when most systems are automated. But really, that's only because I don't want it to end. I love every hour I've spent in this world, and I'm excited for future updates or expansions.

In conclusion, the Planet Crafter is great because it lets you be creative, relax, and make progress. It satisfies the needs of builders, engineers, and anyone else who wants to make something ugly beautiful through their own work.

I only played this game to "try it out," but now I'm 45 hours in, proud of my little blue-green planet, and not even close to being ready to leave it behind.

10/10—would definitely terraform again.

Finally, a game worth its overwhelming positive reviews. Not only did the developers speed through early access they listened to feedback and made a more than viable 1.0 update. Look forward to the future here.

I really didn’t know what I was getting into when I bought this. I just wanted a casual game for the steamdeck, saw this title, bought it and figured it would be one of those games I would probably only play once. I could never get into Minecraft or Valheim; not for a lack of trying. Thought this might be similar. 

Hours and days later, I realize this is nothing like those games. There is something strangely tranquil about this game. I get lost in time and have a hard time putting it down. 

It seems boring at first; maybe a bit pointless. You pick up rocks and run for oxygen every few minutes. It’s tedious. You wonder why you’re doing this. What’s the point?

Then you suddenly notice the sky is blue. Lakes are forming. Grass is growing. You didn’t notice this until you turned around. You go into a wreckage and come out. Where did those trees come from? How long have they been there?

Everything about this game is subtle. It’s so subtle that it sneaks up on you. You think you’re alone. Then you discover there is someone out there trying to help you. It’s lovely, and it’s a little sad. You realize that maybe you didn’t want to be here, but you’ll do your best to make it liveable. 

The game gently nudges you in ways that feel natural. Maybe it’s the music. It’s also subtle. It’s nice, and it’s relaxing. 

This game doesn’t seem like much on the surface. The graphics don’t seem all that great at first, but then it turns into something beautiful, and you appreciate it for all its hard work. 

Do yourself a favour. Don’t look anything up. Don’t watch videos of this game, and don’t google anything. I didn’t, and I’m glad I didn’t. 

Be patient and explore it the way it was meant to be explored. 

There are so many small touches in this game. It will guide you where you need to go if you’re paying attention. 

I love this game. I have no idea what I’m doing. Am I doing too much? Am I doing too little? All I know is the world around me is changing, and I was able to survive another day to witness this beautiful evolution that I have awakened. 

I can only hope that I don’t mess this up. I’ve come too far to turn away now. If I fail, I will fall. 

Great game. Love it. There are so many things I didn’t expect. 

I would recommend this to anyone.

Yo get this game, man. If you're missing the thrill you had when you first played Subnautica, this will scratch that itch. It might not seem super promising at first, but it will pull you in. You will feel the joy. I am still in what I think is the mid game. Do yourself a favor and don't watch any videos or pictures of the game, if you can help it. Let it be a surprise.

First of all, despite everyone comparing this to Subnautica, I don't think it's a particularily good comparison to make.
The fact that TPC has no enemies, the feeling of the game is totally different. Exploration is mostly a boring chore since the map looks kind of similar (similarly bland, that is) everywhere and there is no sense of danger at all. And at the few spots where there are special "biomes", the transition is very poorly done. The lighting and the skybox changes so dramatically when walking over the area boundary that it really kills your immersion. The poor graphics of this title don't do the feeling and exploration any favors here. And the random ships and structures you encounter all look the same and offer no sense of wonder when exploring them. All in all, exploration and discovery are the weakest aspects of this game. 

Another very frustrating mechanic is the building. It currently is very badly designed - for example, when you want to remove a door or window, you have to rebuild the entire structure. The set of decorations and placeable features is sorely lacking as well (there's not even indoor walls). To top it off, nothing aligns properly, and most things don't snap in central spots, making aesthetically pleasing builds very frustrating to accomplish. A far cry from Subnauticas simple but very pleasing building mechanics.

However, I would still recommend this game because it also does some thing extremely well. For example, the core gameplay loop of farming and gathering -> improving your equipment and machines -> exploring and unlocking -> farming and gathering again is very similar to Subnautica, making it rewarding and well balanced. The game has you always wanting to accomplish the next milestone or unlock the next machine.

The terraforming is also a really cool feature, if not the standout feature of this game. Seeing the world slowly come to life through your actions is really rewarding and well designed. A truly unique feature as well.

All in all, this game is very good at hitting the spot of wanting to do "just one more thing" and keeps you engaged this way. The terraforming mechanic is unique and rewarding. But if you are easily distracted by cheap graphics, lack of polish, bugs, and repetitive farming tasks, the bad might outweigh the good for you here. And if you expect Subnautica-esque emergent storytelling or harrowing encounters with terrifying alien fauna, look elsewhere.

Obligatory reminder that this is an Early Access title, things will probably improve, and there have been big updates and good developer interactions in the past.

Outstandingly polished, adaptively paced and engaging throughout. 
Even if you don't like the genre, this one is special and worth a look.

Due to its clever pacing, there's always something to do, no matter if you go fast or if you take your time. The game never overwhelms with too many new mechanics at once, while allowing experienced players to quickly make progress.

Multiplayer pacing and coop is done very well, with an easy drop-in-drop-out system, people can visit your world and join you in building — keeping their inventory between sessions. The pacing beautifully adapts to multiplayer as well, and given the variety of tasks, folks will be able to work together in a very organic way. Be it going out on a big exploration adventure together, or someone designing and beautifying the base while others gather resources.

The first impression the game gives might be is its weakest point. The world might look a tad random and cheap at first, with resource blobs scattered around. It thankfully rather quickly shows how well it was crafted by guiding the player, purely through its design, to the next objectives and opportunities in a very unintrusive manner. As the world is undergoing many terraforming iterations, in the mid-game it further shows how well put together it was.

The unlocking mechanics are a combination of incremental games and exploration that allow each player to go at their pace without getting bored or overwhelmed. The system used here, and the math put it to make it work, is truly commendable and something I hope other devs learn from.

Definitely a good game, and does a good job of feeling like you're terraforming a planet.

There's only a little bit of storyline, and the worldbuilding elements are a little bit iffy if you start thinking about them too hard, but let's be honest, you're not playing this for the story. What there is for story is done fairly competently, nothing too amazing, but nothing really bad either, with a few amusing parts to find.

The important part is you're a convict, you chose to do the high-risk job of terraforming a planet instead of life in prison/execution. You get unceremoniously dumped onto a place that looks basically like Mars when you first get there, with red dirt, dust storms, and no real atmosphere to speak of.

In time, you bring blue skies, water, plant life, and a thriving ecosystem, while discovering the planet's secrets about why there's such an oddly high number of starship crash sites on this outer space bermuda triangle of a planet.

It's not the prettiest game, even on its highest settings, but even with a junker computer you can still run the game well, and it does what it needs to well enough visually. You definitely do see the world change gradually over time based on what you've done, with some more generic, global changes, and some more specific, localised changes based on what you do.

It has a lot of exploration elements of different biomes, various wrecked ships, and even now has a random dungeon generation setup for late game where it can procedurally generate starship wrecks to explore to your heart's desire.

It's still getting continual updates and quality of life patches, and a new planet was added recently as DLC which I have yet to try, but I'll post about that when I play through it on the DLC page.

Overall, it's a game I've played quite a few times, though I'd previously been streaming for various different groups so stopped short of finishing each time. I finally finished it this time through and it's pretty satisfying, with about 30-40 hours worth of content, though it has plenty of replay value as well.

There's also multiplayer added recently, though I have yet to try that, so I can't comment on how effective it is, but it should make an already enjoyable game that much better.

There are a few minor issues, but not many. Occasionally, especially near the end of the game, there are a few "guide-dang-it" moments where it's not really clear what you're supposed to be doing, such as trying to make your first mammals, which don't show up naturally on their own like everything else up to that point and the interface for them is less than clear on how it works.

Setting up automation is a powerful tool, but shows up too late in the game to really matter much and is a massive resource drain for even minimal automation until you're pretty much to the point that resources just don't matter any longer.

The trade rocket is also kind of a problem where almost all of the money you'll get to spend will come from chests via exploration, rather than from anything you trade on your end, because anything you can create is worth about 1/10th or less what it really should be for the effort you put into building it. You can still get plenty of money from exploration, it just feels bad that there's really not much point in building a properly automated factory to produce and trade goods because by the time you get it set up, you'd be at the end of the game anyway and it would have minimal impact.

There are also some issues with clipping through walls sometimes, especially in areas where there's meant to be scripted events later in the game, and a variety of other minor bugs, but nothing gamebreaking.

There's also other minor balance issues like the truck when you first get it just isn't really useful because of the severely reduced mobility compared to the jetpack, though it does become useful for a while after some expensive upgrades to it, but then you have a teleporter network set up and it goes back to being not really useful any longer again because the world just flat out isn't ideal for using a vehicle that can't fly. You can build roads to fix this, but the time and resources spent doing so would again be wasted because it'd just be faster not to do that in the first place.

These are, however, minor gripes. They're nitpicking at best. The game is extremely good and a solid AA-tier game, just don't expect AAA-tier visuals or attention to detail. For what it is, it's amazing and well worth the full asking price, even without a sale. With a sale, there's really no reason not to buy it if you like exploration/crafting-survival games.

Note there are no monsters in the game at all. No enemies. No guns. Your only threats are things like falling from high heights until you get a jetpack, a lack of food, or a lack of water or oxygen, and these become mostly trivial to deal with after about a third of the way through the game or so. As such, it's really not a "hard" game by any means, so don't come looking for a challenge because you won't really find one here. It's just a very pleasant, relaxing game to explore and terraform a planet to nice music. If that's what you want, you will find exactly that.

Edit: Forgot to mention, there are currently 3 endings to be discovered, depending on what you value. They're not hugely different from each other, and are like 1990s-era level of being basically a basic animation and a few lines of text. If you hated the ending to Starcraft 2, then basically this is more of that, but on an even smaller scale. Again, minor gripe, you didn't come here for the story, you came here to craft a planet, and the endings do show off your planet from a nice vantage point.

Alright. [i]The Planet Crafter[/i] is done and dusted. I saw two of the three endings. Not exactly certain what triggers the third, but I was ready to be finished after sixty hours anyway, so I'll probably just watch the third on YT. I spent $16.79 on this during the recent Steam Open World Survival Crafting Fest, and that was a stellar price for this amount of content. I did play this solo, and it's definitely perfectly suited to solo play. However, I would imagine having a crew playing this together would expedite things, especially in the later terraforming stages where the game can drag on a bit.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3267702822

So, you play as a person convicted of a crime that isn't specified, but the implication is that Sentinel Corp, the human corporate government, is not averse to inflating minor crimes into death sentences and then convincing the convicts to accept the almost certain death sentence of terraforming a lifeless planet in exchange for commuting the sentences afterwards. And that is the position you find yourself in. You are dropped onto a lifeless planet with only your trusty multitool gun thingy (the name of which escapes me lol) and a will to survive. Initially, survival will be very difficult since you will have to find food, water, and oxygen wherever you can, and it can be a desperate struggle. As you progress, and especially once you reach certain stages of terraforming, these things stop being a factor. 

After exploring a bit and starting to create livable circumstances for yourself, you will really focus on both terraforming and long range exploration, becoming more familiar with the planet even as the planet becomes more livable. This can be pretty exciting at times. The actual act of mining and finding supplies, building your base, and so on, isn't much to write home about, but exploring your first wrecks, finding logs left by other people who had the misfortune of crashing here (or being sent here as a criminal just like you), watching the actual stages of terraforming coming to fruition....those are all pretty inspiring moments that carry a sense of pride and satisfaction. Finding evidence of previous intelligent life on the planet is about as cool as it gets and sets the foundation for the second main plot line, which was kind of awesome. The first being your endeavor to terraform this planet and GTFO of course. One of the things you find talks about how humans evolve in similar fashion under similar conditions regardless of how far apart they are, and the only significant difference at that point is how they think and process information. Which is something I have long considered to be true.

Eventually, you will unlock teleporters, and that basically changes everything. You can easily set up mining operations in key areas, set up teleporters in other areas you deem important, and it really keeps you from having to continue with the super long treks that are part and parcel with this game. 

Graphically, what begins as a drab and mostly featureless experience morphs into something completely different as the world starts to change and become more alive. The use of contrast and a full color palette to differentiate between biomes and the circumstances within said biomes was nicely done. There was one area I called "The Moon" in my playthrough that was so visually striking that I just sat there taking it in for minute. The plant life was all really imaginative and the designs really enhanced the world. Additionally, there are some secret areas in the game that are flat out stunning and super cool looking. The planet provides an interesting dichotomy between what begins as basically lifeless desert and transforms into lakes, forests and jungles, and even an ocean.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3268789616

The audio is all activity driven with a musical score in the background that was pretty much ripped straight from Mass Effect. It's nice and all, but not particularly noteworthy outside of some suspect borrowing of the Mass Effect series trademark soundtrack, with some minor tweaks. It's not one for one, but anyone who has played both will find the inspiration undeniable.

What I did not particularly enjoy was exploring the higher difficulty ships. Difficulty in this instance directly correlates to how mazelike a ship is. However, if you've seen one ship, you've seen them all, the rewards aren't super compelling despite finding necessary crafting stuff, flares are kind of costly to craft and use as markers, and I just didn't really enjoy this much at all after like the third or fourth ship. Even when you unlock portals that allow you to find new ships and select which ships you'd like to try to find knowing their difficulty ahead of time, this didn't alter anything other than enhancing the value of the things you can find exploring said ships.

And there are definitely some bugs in this game. Most noteworthy is how you can and will end up inside of mountains and such because the game couldn't render the assets faster than you could arrive at them. Once, this resulted in my finding a secret area but also being trapped in it since I had entered through what looked like more mountain but after it rendered in, was actually a gap in the floor/ceiling (depending on which way you look at it from), rather than from unlocking a door as intended. Rendering speed seems to be the culprit for pretty much all the bugs I personally encountered with two exceptions. It's fine, it's fine, it's fine and then suddenly it's not. Another issue I encountered was some stuttering and moments where the game would just flat out freeze. And finally, every so often, some crafting material would get stuck in the ground or a wall and would be impervious to my efforts to claim it.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3267702805

I tried this with both the Steam Deck and an Xbox X controller and didn't really like how the game played using either. I switched to k/m and it became a pretty seamless experience from a gameplay perspective from that point on.

I think the game was a lot of fun and I enjoyed my stay for the most part. It did perhaps run about five hours longer than I would have liked, and I found myself idling through a lot of the final stage, just checking in to feed and water my character periodically. I'd had my fill of exploration and builder tasks by then. But the sense of awe when finding alien ruins and secret areas, and the feeling of satisfaction and of just flat-out pride when you see the effects of your efforts throughout the world really override any issues I had with the game. It's capable of bringing out all your favorite emotions, and for that, I am thankful to have had the opportunity to play this game.  The price is certainly more than fair for the amount of content, and I think if you play this with friends, it could only enhance that experience further. Give it a look for sure.

I saw this game and thought that it looked like Subnautica, which was reinforced to me by the "Similar to games you've played section" on steam. This framed the game to me as above ground Subnautica with online multiplayer. While not entirely inaccurate, this affected my experience in a way that wasn't entirely beneficial. 

This game is more similar at it's core to games like cookie clicker than Subnautica. That might sound strange but the main gameplay loop here is building drills, heaters, oxygen generating machines etc. which act as generators that add to your pressure, heat, oxygen, and overall terraformation index numbers. As these numbers grow you unlock better equipment, better machines and this feeds into a very enjoyable positive feedback loop of exponential growth. This can be very extremely satisfying, and the world changes as you hit certain milestones and which is great to see. It really feels like you are crafting this planet. 

The people I was playing with told me it's very similar to satisfactory, without managing pipelines etc, but I haven't played that yet and to me the loop seemed similar to idle clicker games, just with more to do. Obviously it includes all the other survival game things of managing hunger, thirst and oxygen and building and designing your base.

The reason I mention Subnautica and how it affected my experience is I was expecting exploration to be a similar focus to how it is in Subnautica. Exploring the world was the best, and main, gameplay in that game after all. The Planet Crafter does have some exploration, and it is fairly enjoyable, but it is also clearly the least developed part of the game. Many of the rocks and spaceships you can find don't have completely accurate collision detection so it is fairly common to fall through rocks, especially if you try to travel via ways the developers did not intend, for example over the rocks that separate the different areas. There also simply wasn't as much work put into making the world as interesting to explore as a game like Subnautica and, while not necessarily a flaw, it was the most disappointing aspect of the game for me. 

There were still some cool things to find and I enjoyed running back though some areas later to see how the world changed as we terraformed it, but it is still easily the weakest part of the game.

At first glance, Planet Crafter may not seem all that impressive. Its graphics are a bit rough, and the visuals won’t blow you away. But trust me, once you dive in, it quickly becomes one of the most addictive games I’ve ever played.

You start the game fighting for survival. Every expedition outside your safe haven is a real risk, as you scavenge for materials on a barren, desolate planet. But this struggle is also where the game shines. The progression is perfectly paced, you’re always overcoming obstacles, reaching a milestone that makes things easier, only to face new challenges that push you further. Surviving, gathering resources, and exploring all come with their own difficulties, but as you improve, there’s a constant sense of reward. Just as things start to feel routine, a new milestone reinvigorates the experience, keeping it fresh and engaging.

And if that wasn’t satisfying enough, Planet Crafter takes progression a step further by allowing you to witness your direct impact on the world. What begins as a lifeless desert slowly transforms into a lush, thriving paradise, all thanks to your hard work. Few games make you feel this accomplished.

The multiplayer aspect is also a huge plus, allowing up to ten players. While it’s enjoyable solo, the experience is undoubtedly best with friends.

That said, the game isn’t without flaws. The graphics, while functional, can feel inconsistent, with certain textures and effects not blending smoothly into the environment. There are also occasional graphical bugs, such as areas where players can clip through terrain. While I don’t expect photorealism, a bit more polish would go a long way.

Some players have also criticized the game’s scientific inaccuracies. But honestly, Planet Crafter prioritizes fun and engagement over realism, and that’s a trade-off I’m happy to accept.

Despite its rough edges, Planet Crafter delivers one of the most rewarding and engaging gameplay experiences out there. If you can look past its visual shortcomings, you’ll find an incredibly satisfying adventure that keeps you hooked from start to finish.

Final Verdict: 8/10

Why the game is great:
The progression loop: This is its strongest suit. There is a constant stream of rewards. First, the ice melts, then lakes form, then moss starts to grow, and eventually, butterflies are flying around. That visual feedback is incredibly addictive.

(Almost) Zero stress : Unlike many survival games, you don't have to fight zombies or aliens here. Your biggest enemy is your own oxygen meter. It is a relaxing, almost meditative experience.

The scale: You start with a handful of iron and end with giant rockets that blast asteroids out of the sky to collect resources.

Things to consider:
Rather simple graphics: Don't expect hyper-realistic visuals but rather cartoon-style. The game looks decent, but it’s functional rather than breathtaking.

The "Grind": Toward the end of the game, gathering rare resources can sometimes feel repetitive, though automation and drones help alleviate this later on.

Loneliness: You are alone. For some, this is wonderful; for others, the world might feel a bit empty after 30 hours. Unless you play co-op with friends of course!

Who is this for?
If you enjoy Base Building, Automation (like Satisfactory or Factorio, but lighter), and watching a world transform before your eyes, this is a must-play. It is one of the most satisfying "clean-up" games I played before.

This game is the peak example of the dev understanding how games should be built. The graphics, gameplay and mechanics are super forgiving and all just janky enough to allow you to play the game in the way that is the most fun to *you*. Want to glitch through walls and access high-level areas way too early? Absolutely. Want to glitch up walls for a shortcut? Sure. If that's what you want to do, the game just lets you do it. But there's also a creative mode, so...
But what I mean with the devs understanding the players, is that they start out with a relatively bland-looking crafting survival game, but over time introduce more and more mechanics that eliminate the often repetitive parts of crafting and surviving and allow you to focus on the bigger picture of building a base and progressing on the planet. For example:
[spoiler]- Oxygen becomes a non-issue once you reach a breathable atmosphere
- Resources that are initially finite and have to be collected by hand can eventually be crafted or auto-mined
- Inventory management and crates are eventually all auto-sortable with drones
- Crafting chains can be completely automated with auto-crafters that use existing item storage
- Travelling becomes much simpler with a faster vehicle and portals. Also, the map eventually creates natural shortcuts for you.
[/spoiler]
While still being quite linear, the game is full of charming surprises that keep the gameplay fresh and interesting, and rewards the player for progressing instead of punishing them with ever-growing crafting chains. Yes, the late-game has a noticeable change of pace as you realize how much more of *everything* you suddenly need to progress, but it's bearable as you'll probably be discovering the game's lore at the same the same time.
Embrace the jank and enjoy this masterclass of game design! Highly recommended.

After spending a completely totally normal amount of time in a game that I have owned for less than two weeks, I can confidently say that I greatly enjoy Planet Crafter. This game was recommended to me by a friend after I had finished the Subnautica 2 early access content, as I was chomping at the bit for more of that particular brand of Survival Crafting, and wowie did it not disappoint.

[h2]THE PROS:[/h2]

- [b]Gameplay:[/b] Like honestly, just. Everything. The progression is incredible, feels organic, and objective tracking gives that wonderful wonderful bliss of Number Go Up. you start off on a red rock with basic materials and have to survive with a multitool, a few pouches of food, and a bunch of rocks you find on the planet's surface. You start with a short list of getting to your first major terraforming stage, and after that it's all up to you. As you gather materials, you get recipes from your totally benevolent corporate overlords for more advanced machines and equipment upgrades. Use them to explore further the planet you've landed on, find higher-tier materials, and build the ever increasing list of machines and base modules to turn this seemingly desolate red rock into a habitable planet with a breathable atmosphere.

- [b]Controls and UI:[/b] Largely intuitive. Point and click to gather resources. I think I did the first time have to check which button was bound to the build menu, but that may also have been because my neurotic fool self missed the prompt on the screen. I genuinely can't remember. It's Q by default if you're on keyboard by the way. Menus are solidly organized and generally easy to navigate.

- [b]Story:[/b] YEAH BABY THERE'S A STORY AND IT'S MORE THAN JUST "your job is make planet nice, godspeed :)" AND IT SLAPS!!! IT SLAPS HARD!!! From the go it's hinted at, but as you explore and progress and Make Discoveries, it all unfolds in a WONDERFULLY satisfying way, and it is a very mild (but very good!!) horror story. No jumpscares, just some nice creeping dread and dawning horrific implications. Chef's kiss all around.

- [b]The DLC:[/b] I have only finished one of the extra planets (Humble), but if you like the base game, you will like the other planets. You get to go to the other moons and planets in the solar system after a certain point deep in late game, and it does not disappoint. Behold once more the joy of Number Go Up, AND each planet comes with its own unique story line! The DLC planets can also be picked as starting points for the beginning of a new game, but in all honesty I think that should be reserved for challenge runs.

- [b]The Performance:[/b] Solid all around. My coplayer and I have had a little bit of weird and wiggy graphical things every so often (I once found a cliff that did not actually exist, that was wild), but honestly that is to be expected on such a large scale game made by two whole people. The game is still being updated, and I have confidence that anything major will be quickly rectified, because that's what someone who loves their craft like I can feel in this game does. The game runs well, I had one crash one time when my computer was already acting a fool. My coplayer has never had issues with connecting, we have never suffered lag, I have never launched this game and been concerned about technical tomfoolery.

[h2]THE CONS:[/h2]

- Ok I'm probably gonna have to reach into the very bowels of haterism for this because in my humble opinion this game is basically tailor made for me specifically. But no game is perfect, and to claim perfection is BIAS. I will NOT be biased, this review WILL be meaningful and not baseless glazing!

The very worst things I can think of in this game are two mildly annoying crafting grievences: a couple of later game upgrades feel like they should maybe be base game QOL features.

Very specifically, you have to craft equipment upgrades and use equipment slots to pin blueprints and to hide low-level machines. Considering some machines go up to level 5, and every one is literal ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE better than the tier below it in every way, I can make searching through your crafting menu in mid-game a little annoying.

The blueprint thing is annoying because certain recipes can only be crafted from certain items (for example, you can only craft rockets on the rocket launch pad). This would be fine, except you can also only SEE the recipe from those crafting stations as well. So for more complex recipes, if you don't have the blueprint pin chip, you kinda just have to hope you remember everything, take a manual pic, or run back and forth between storage and the crafting station to remember ingredients.

Like I said, annoying, but ultimately, nothing that truly infringes upon my joy of the game.

THAT'S IT. THAT'S ALL I GOT. I genuinely have nothing left to nitpick, I enjoy literally every aspect of this game, it tickles everything I love about survival crafting games, it has one of my personal favorite setting and atmospheres (isolation in space/an alien planet), and some of the best game progression I've ever seen.

Get the game. Get it. GEEEETTTTT ITTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTT

I would like to give a "neutral" thumb.

At first, it's pretty ok. You are runnig around and gather resources around you to build shelter and
automate your critical items.
Then you care about actual terraforming.

But....
The main gameplay loop was not engaging to me in the mid game.
I played until about 60% to "Lake" stage at this point.
There is a lot more to come.
You do get better/faster ways of moving, but you still run around at this stage and
round-trip through your other bases where your drills are.
You need to manually go there and empty them and bring the stuff to where you craft your stuff,
or they will stop working.
Loot the next ship here. Launch a rocket there.
So most of your time you are using your hover-jetpack to visit those places, bring stuff to your base, manually sort it,
craft and build more stuff to accelerate the terraforming.
The unlocks you make are tied to the 10-ish different terraforming progress counters.
So you need to balance them to get the more important machines.
Now, this all sounds well and good.
But the fact that 10 hours into the game, I still cannot automate anything, still have to manually visit all those places
for the 500th time, still have to build more of the same, or replace old stuff with Tier+1 stuff to make progress not
getting shallow is kinda tiresome.
Each upgrade you unlock takes about 3-10 times the amount of terraforming progress than the previous.
So you need to keep up by building the newest stuff and launching rockets to get a bonus for the different areas.
But your workload just rises and rises and rises.
You need to hit the endgame to unlock stuff that actually reduces your workload again.(Drones ect)
But after early game, nothing you build will benefit YOU.
The only reward you get, is slightly better gear to be faster doing ... more manual labor before the sun sets.

If I play a survival game, I want my life to get easier with progress. Automate resources.

And I'm not willing to play another 10 or 20 hours to finally get to Drone stage to make my life easier again.

But don't expect to ever having more time to see, what you have created so far.

You constantly need to be on your toes to do more of the same with your own hands.
Might be for you. It's not for me.

[h1]The Planet Crafter Review [/h1]

[b]The objective[/b]
This game is very simple, you landed on a barren planet with many other crashed spaceships. You need to gather recources to inprove air quality and temperature so that lakes will form and plants will grow.

[b]Graphics[/b]
The graphics of this game look incredibly cool, the scenery is epic and the lighting looks good (I use Ultra settings, but even high and medium look awsome). As a person who likes landscapes I couldn't be happier with the view of this land. The graphics also keep inproving with the game after your planet inproves to a lovely place.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
If you like looking around and building stuff, this is the game for you. You can search pretty much any place and find cool stuff if you look hard enough. The constant inproving of your place is very rewarding to look at aswell.

[b]Audio[/b]
I am honestly not the best person to descibe audio, but the sounds that have been put in this game do fit the game very well, giving a calming feeling while you look for all the necicary recources. The sound feels emersive and very well placed.

[b]Audience[/b]
This game can be played by anyone, just don't expect a competitive or PvE experience.

[b]PC recuirements[/b]
You are just fine if you have a decently recent pc. 4GB VRAM and pretty much any CPU should be enough. I'd say: 'If you can run Minecraft, you can run this'

[b]Difficulty[/b]
This game has multiple difficulties. You can choose the gamemode that is very relaxing, forgiving and easy, where the objective is just to have some fun with exploring and building. The standard difficulty is still pretty forgiving, since you can still get your items back after death, which isn't the case with the harder two modes, where you also die a lost faster. Lastly you have the hardcore mode, where you just have one life and death is the end of this run.

[b]Grind[/b]
If you like grinding a game, this game could be for you, but grinding isn't necessary. You can plant down some ore generators for the common items and craft more complex things from that. There are some rare items though, which you have to look for in the open world. Most items don't need more that 6 items to build, so even to being creative grinding is not a big obstacle.

[b]Story[/b]
As far as I know, there is not a lot of story in this game. Being a sandbox game I wouldn't expect anything else. You do get some messages every once in a while, but I don't feel like they really deepen the lore.

[b]Gametime[/b]
Technically you can play this game infinitely, but after you built everything you wanted and unlocked everything it could become a bit boring. But unlocking all the items and world events will take at least 10 hours, and if you take building with that, you could drag it up to 30 to even 50 hours per world.

[b]Price[/b]
I'd definetely recommend buying this game if you like adventuring and being creative. It is not a very expensive game (currently about $16), yet it is very fun and exiting to play.

[b]Bugs[/b]
Being still in the early access, the game has some bugs, but that is to be expected. It mostly has hitbox bugs with some high up objects, so it would be hard to get there anyway.

[b]Final rating[/b]
If this were a fully released and refined game, I would give this game an 8/10, but I can see that the developers are still putting lots of time in the game and I'm exited to see the future. So my final score would be a 9/10, which is very inpressive in my book.

It’s honestly a breath of fresh air that in a gaming landscape dominated by shooting, conquering, and overall digital destruction, we have a gem like this. You play a lone pioneer, dropped onto a desolate, dusty rock with a single, massive mandate: turn this hostile wasteland into a thriving paradise, or run out of oxygen trying. It is a game entirely about healing rather than hurting.

I am posting this review at about 65 hours, which is not a tonne of time compared to what some people pour into these massive builders. I am only about halfway through my very first playthrough, but I am absolutely loving it.

Your journey begins in the absolute dirt. Armed with nothing but a handy construction tool and a dream, you start vacuuming up raw minerals to piece together basic survival gear, heaters, and atmospheric drills. Yes, you have to ignore the fact that a few small machines can warm up an entire planet and create an atmosphere in a matter of hours, but that is the beauty of this sci fi setup. It trades tedious, real time centuries for a satisfyingly accelerated power trip where you can watch the ice melt and the pressure rise right before your eyes.

Before long, the landscape begins to shift, and you move on to biology. That orange, dusty ground gives way to a faint green fuzz of moss, which soon blossoms into fields of wild grass and vibrant flowers. Next thing you know, you are breeding exotic butterflies, dropping fish into newly formed lakes, and eventually splicing genetic material to grow adorable bioengineered creatures to roam your greening pastures. Watching life literally erupt from a place that once had absolutely nothing is incredibly satisfying, and yes, petting your new creations is highly encouraged.

The expansions and extra content keep the momentum going beautifully. Planet Humble offers a fantastic change of pace with its gorgeous, distinct biomes and fresh mining twists, while the Toxic DLC challenges you with a sickly, polluted environment that desperately needs some serious environmental care. Throw in the free moons and late game interstellar portals that let you jet off to bizarre new frontiers, and there is no shortage of projects to tackle. Whether you like to push one massive save file to its absolute limits or restart fresh to optimize your build order, the game happily accommodates your playstyle.

The core gameplay loop has a wonderfully hypnotic quality. You will lose hours to it without even realizing. You will set out to build a new tier of machinery, get distracted by an eerie shipwreck, forget why you have an inventory full of magnesium, and wind up launching a giant rocket into space instead. Speaking of which, shooting satellites into the sky to artificially multiply your terraformation speed is a brilliant touch that always keeps the progress bars ticking upward. There is always a goal to chase.

Exploring the map is a genuine treat, too. Wandering into deep, glowing caves or exploring abandoned bases always yields exactly what you need to take that next big technological leap. The game’s progression curve is masterfully tuned. Just when you think you have hit a wall, you find a cache of rare materials or unlock a blueprint that completely changes how you build.

Ultimately, The Planet Crafter is a deeply rewarding, massive experience packed with charm. Seeing the sky slowly change from a toxic orange to a brilliant, watery blue, complete with clouds and falling rain, is a visual payoff that few games can match. It can get a bit complex and slightly repetitive in the late game automation phase, but if you are looking for a peaceful, satisfying builder that lets you leave a world better than you found it, this is an absolute must play.

Highly recommended!

The first thing I want to mention:
No, this is NOT Subnautica in space. I don't know why people latch so much on these superficial comparisons between the games. Yes, there are wrecks. Yes you need to grab resources and unlock blueprints. But this does not make a game Subnautica. The gameplay loop is completely different.

Your goal in Planet Crafter is to reach a certain terraforming score, which essentially means this is an "incremental" builder game. Anything you work towards to is to be more efficient at gaining score in arbitrarily chosen categories (O2 , Heat, Pressure, Biomass) I do hope these get reworked to be at least semi balanced because having only O2 as your atmosphere is a very bad thing. :P

Nitpicks aside, this is still a fun gameplay loop experience. You start off with almost nothing and have to first expand your equipment so you can actually start to build. From there the loop is basically:

- Invest resources into buildings to accumulate more score to gain unlocks to gain points more efficiently
- Explore the map to find resources you need for these
- Eventually see results of your "Terraforming"

It's pretty relaxing, a good podcast game. So if you think you'd enjoy this kind of gameplay loops, then the game is for you. At the moment of when this review was written I'd say the main downsides are:
- Garish color palette thats way oversaturated
- Lots of clipping bugs, its very easy to leave the playable game area.
- No animations / feedback for the player character. You're always a static gun arm with almost no movement.
- Resources are just randomly placed all over the map, it looks very weird/lazy.
- Performance tanks if you actually start to plant greenery.

I’ve been thinking about buying The Planet Crafter for quite some time, and during the autumn sales I finally decided to give it a try — and honestly, it’s one of the best decisions I’ve made in a long time. From the very first moments, I was completely drawn in.

The game offers an incredibly satisfying loop of exploring, crafting, and farming resources. Every new machine you build and every upgrade you unlock gives you the feeling that you’re genuinely shaping the world around you. Terraforming might be a slow process, but that’s exactly what makes it so rewarding: watching a cold, empty planet slowly turn into something alive and thriving because of your actions.

The progression is beautifully immersive. In the beginning, you’re just trying to survive, counting every piece of iron and every breath of oxygen. But as time goes on, your base grows, your production expands, and suddenly you’re building massive structures and seeing the planet come to life. It’s an amazing feeling to look back and realize how far you’ve come.

The atmosphere is another thing that makes this game special. Even though it’s technically a survival game, it never feels overwhelming. The world changes around you at its own pace, and the ambient music perfectly enhances the calm and immersive experience.

On a more personal note — I’m dealing with a serious medical condition and a lot of daily pain. This game has become more than just entertainment for me. It gives me a way to escape for a while, to focus on something creative and peaceful instead of the constant pain and stress. It’s incredibly therapeutic to lose myself in this world and see it grow with every small step I take.

And with up to ten-player multiplayer, I can only imagine how amazing it must be to build an entire world together with friends. Even solo, though, it’s been an unforgettable journey.

If you love crafting, base-building, resource management, or simply the feeling of watching something beautiful take shape over time, this game is absolutely worth it. It’s relaxing, rewarding, and surprisingly emotional in the best possible way.

I hesitated for a while before buying it, but now I can say with complete certainty: I love this game.
